solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Secret clique led by Democrat in China?

indicators.note: whatever is led by something has that thing walking at its front

parts.note: inner = private, secret, as in inner thoughts

explanation.surface: A secretive political faction run by a Democrat operating in China.
explanation.walkthrough: China is capitalised only because it opens the sentence's last phrase; the question mark warns that it means crockery, not the country.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a dinner set is a matching service of plates and dishes, typically made of china.

clue.text: Her son goes crazy with daughter ahead in polls

indicators.note: something ahead is out in front
letters that go crazy lose their sane order and are rearranged

explanation.surface: A mother's son behaves wildly while his sister leads in the opinion polls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polls' looks like elections, but to poll cattle is a farming term for cutting off their horns.
explanation.definitionFit: A farming sense: to poll cattle is to remove their horns, the same job as dehorning.

indicators.note: letters banned at regular intervals means every other one is thrown out

parts.note: the even letters of aNd OrGy

explanation.surface: Drink and debauchery are both prohibited by some regular rule.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And' looks like a link word but is part of the letter string: the kept letters run across both words.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: nog is a strong ale from East Anglia, and also short for eggnog.

indicators.note: a building that houses something holds it inside, so the estate holds I'M

parts.note: a manor is a landed estate
one is = I am, contracted to I'm

explanation.surface: A question of what someone's manor house is worth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One's' reads as possessive, but here it is 'one is': the speaker is the one, so I AM, shortened to I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are verbs of appraisal: to value a house is to put a figure on its worth.

explanation.surface: A complaint that there is little time for studying.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads the whole clue as one complaint about a short revision period; in fact 'Not much' is the definition and the rest is the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, used before a noun: scant attention is not much attention.

clue.text: Sign for staff meaning break cut short

parts.note: the tenor of something is its general meaning

indicators.note: cut short means the last letter is removed

parts.note: a cleft is a break or split

explanation.surface: A notice for employees explains the meaning of a curtailed break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'staff' looks like employees; it is the musical stave. CLEFT loses its last T.
explanation.definitionFit: A clef is a symbol placed on a musical stave to fix the pitch of the notes.

clue.text: Old lady on organ is hot stuff

indicators.note: in an across clue, something sitting on another thing comes after it

parts.note: an organ is a publication, a magazine or mag
one's old lady = one's mother, ma

explanation.surface: An elderly woman at the church organ is a sensation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organ' suggests music or anatomy; it is a periodical, as in 'the party organ'.
explanation.definitionFit: A literal reading of a slang phrase: magma is molten rock, stuff that really is hot.

clue.text: Dog biting American man's backside for sport

indicators.note: the dog word bites into the other pieces, holding them inside

parts.note: a mutt is a mongrel dog

indicators.note: a backside is the rear, so the final letter

explanation.surface: A dog nips an American's bottom just for fun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sport' is the biological sense: an organism differing markedly from its parent stock.
explanation.definitionFit: In biology a sport is an individual showing a sudden genetic variation, a mutant.

clue.text: Force poor navigator to adopt new way of processing data

indicators.note: adopting means taking in, so the rearranged letters hold the other piece
poor means the letters of navigator are in a bad, jumbled order

parts.note: IT, information technology, is the modern way of handling data

explanation.surface: An incompetent navigator is made to learn a new computer system.
explanation.walkthrough: IT, information technology, is the 'new way of processing data'; the rearranged navigator letters take it in.
explanation.definitionFit: Gravitation is the attractive force between masses.

indicators.note: one thing after another comes later in the line

parts.note: F is foxtrot in the phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A touch of swagger after dancing a superb foxtrot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slight' reads as an adjective meaning small, but it is the noun meaning an insult.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym once 'slight' is read as a noun: a snub or insult to someone's dignity.

definitions.meaning: surface: a verb, someone having a meal; meant: the slang noun for food
when that food is served: late in the day

explanation.walkthrough: 'Eats' looks like a verb, someone dining; it is the slang noun for food. High tea is a British early-evening meal of cooked food with tea.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: the meal taken late in the afternoon, with cooked dishes as well as cake.

definitions.meaning: an emphatic yes, in British slang
taken literally: the half is negated, switched off

explanation.surface: An emphatic assurance that the sale really is half price.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' is British slang for an enthusiastic yes; the second reading takes the phrase literally.
explanation.definitionFit: A British idiom: 'Did you enjoy it?' 'Not half!' means definitely; literally, a half is not there.

indicators.note: something covered in sheets is wrapped inside them

parts.note: a ream is 500 sheets of paper

explanation.surface: A stretch of ground left blanketed under sheets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sheets' suggests bedding or rain; it is paper, counted in reams.
explanation.definitionFit: Area in the figurative sense, a field of interest, as in 'the realm of science'.

indicators.note: naughty letters misbehave and will not stay in order

explanation.surface: A wayward girl who is crazy about sherry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mad' looks like a second anagram signal, but it is fodder; 'Naughty' does the stirring.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: amontillado is a medium-dry style of Spanish sherry.

clue.text: He directs opening of Titanic, remade on a train

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter
a film remade is made again differently, so the letters are rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: A film director reshoots the start of Titanic set on a train.
explanation.walkthrough: The film-making surface points at James Cameron, but the director wanted is Quentin Tarantino.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Quentin Tarantino is a film director, so he directs.

explanation.surface: A Broadway show's run was cut short, leaving money owed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Season on Broadway' suggests a theatre run; it is simply the American word for autumn.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from accounting: the amount by which money falls short of what is needed.

clue.text: British leaving African capital, lost and in distress

indicators.note: leaving means the abbreviation for British departs from the capital's name

parts.note: Bangui is the capital of the Central African Republic
to shed something is to lose it

explanation.surface: A Briton who has left an African city, lost and distressed.
explanation.definitionFit: Anguished describes someone suffering severe mental pain, so they are in distress.

parts.note: to savage a show is to pan it

indicators.note: the beast's last is its final letter

explanation.surface: A wild animal's dying breath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Savage beast' reads as one phrase; 'Savage' is a verb meaning to criticise harshly.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs describe short, laboured breathing.

clue.text: Wool caught on tree by lake

indicators.note: in a down clue, a thing on another sits above it

explanation.surface: A tuft of fleece snagged on a lakeside tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught' is not the wool snagging but the cricket scorer's c; 'mere' is an old word common in English place names.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: cashmere is the fine wool of the Kashmir goat.

clue.text: See you in transit at airport

indicators.note: the answer sits in the words that follow, straddling them

explanation.surface: A goodbye said to someone passing through an airport.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across three words, which is why 'at' looks like innocent filler.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are casual British farewells.

clue.text: Understood issue coming up in the past

indicators.note: in a down clue, something coming up travels upwards, so it reads bottom to top

parts.note: 'I see' means I understand, so saw = understood

explanation.surface: A matter that was grasped when it came up earlier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Issue' reads as a topic under discussion, and 'coming up' as it arising; both words are doing mechanical work, and the reversal takes in the whole string, not just the second part.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: 'time was when...' means there was a time, in the past, when.

parts.note: bull and guff both mean nonsense

explanation.surface: A bull that is both impressive and hilarious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bull' is not an animal but nonsense; 'inspiring' looks like a container instruction but is part of the phrase for AWING.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer as a verbal noun: a loud, hearty kind of laughter.

indicators.note: the cycled word goes in the valley word

parts.note: a glen is a narrow Scottish valley

indicators.note: cycling means the first letter goes round to the end

explanation.surface: A cheer goes up for dad as he cycles through a valley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cycling' looks like dad riding a bike, but it moves a letter of dad from the front to the back. A glen is a Scottish valley.
explanation.definitionFit: To gladden is to make happy, to cheer someone up.

parts.note: an ism is a doctrine or teaching

explanation.surface: A department of a school's teaching staff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Division' reads as a school department; it is a split, especially within a church.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a split within a group into opposing factions, classically a church.

clue.text: Guy charged with current murder is copper's source

indicators.note: charged with means filled with, so the guy word holds the other pieces

parts.note: a hit is a contract killing

explanation.surface: A man accused of an electrocution killing turns out to be the police officer's informant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copper' looks like a police officer; it is the metal. MALE holds AC+HIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Malachite is a green mineral that is mined as an ore of the metal copper.

indicators.note: the celebrity's second is the letter in second place

explanation.surface: A star's backup private plane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jet' is not a plane but the deep black colour, and 'second spare' is not a backup.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are names for a deep, glossy black, from the mineral and the wood.

indicators.note: without bounds means without the letters at its edges

parts.note: Madras is now officially called Chennai

explanation.surface: The limitless colours of present-day Madras.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Modern' is the key: the city was renamed from Madras in 1996, and only the new name contains the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A dye used as a colour: henna gives hair and skin a reddish-brown tint.

clue.text: Rather frail married couple welcoming each brief kiss

indicators.note: welcoming means taking in, so the couple's letters surround the rest

parts.note: W and H, the abbreviations for wife and husband

indicators.note: brief means cut short, losing the last letter

explanation.surface: A frail husband and wife greet one another with a quick peck.
explanation.walkthrough: W (wife) and H (husband) surround EA plus KIS (kiss cut short).
explanation.definitionFit: Weakish means somewhat weak, so a little feeble or frail.

clue.text: Half-blind from love, yet endlessly in distress

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it
'endlessly' cuts a letter off

explanation.surface: Blinded by love and still desperate: a lovesick lament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In distress' looks like one phrase meaning upset, which tempts a solver to hunt for an anagram; 'in' is a placement instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A playful definition: with one eye you have half your sight, so half-blind.

indicators.note: read aloud means the letter's spoken name gives the answer

explanation.surface: A single letter is being read out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' is the impersonal pronoun, as in 'one never knows', which can be replaced by 'you'.
explanation.definitionFit: Generic 'you' and formal 'one' are both pronouns for people in general.

clue.text: Charge round room after case of stout

indicators.note: what comes after follows in the line
a word's case is its outer shell, its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A fee for delivering a crate of stout round to someone's room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case of stout' suggests a crate of beer; it means the outside letters of the word. 'Charge' is an attack, not a fee.
explanation.definitionFit: A military sense: to storm a position is to rush at and attack it.

indicators.note: pickled means drunk, so the letters stagger into a new order

explanation.surface: A menu offering pickled nuts: dull food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fare' looks like food, fitting the pickled nut; it is a ticket price. A day return is a British rail ticket out and back on the same day.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: a day return is one kind of ticket price charged by British railways.
